messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This looks to be a bug in poppr. I've flagged it as an issue on poppr's GitHub page [0] and it will be fixed in the next release.
In the meantime, a workaround would be to set a population for your data:

pop(genind) <- rep("A", nInd(genind))

Unrelated, but I additionally recommend to not use function names ("genind") as variable names.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

Hello,

I've recently run into some difficulty with large data sets (>5000 individuals with 14 microsatellite loci) when attempting to run AMOVAs using the poppr.amova() function. I'm curious if there are limits to the number of individuals or the size of the genind object that this function is capable of handling? These same data sets are processed in Arlequin rather quickly so it's puzzling to me why R/poppr/ade4 appear to be struggling and throwing errors related to long vectors and requiring RAM availability >40GB. messages.subject: Re: [poppr] data input size or individual number limits for 'poppr' AMOVA analysis
messages.subject_clean: [poppr] data input size or individual number limits for 'poppr' AMOVA analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello Matt,

Thank you for submitting this question to the forum.

> On Apr 4, 2017, at 14:48 , Matthew Fuller <matthew.ro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I've recently run into some difficulty with large data sets (>5000 individuals with 14 microsatellite loci) when attempting to run AMOVAs using the poppr.amova() function. I'm curious if there are limits to the number of individuals or the size of the genind object that this function is capable of handling?

There are no official limits, just the amount of RAM available on your machine.

> These same data sets are processed in Arlequin rather quickly so it's puzzling to me why R/poppr/ade4 appear to be struggling and throwing errors related to long vectors and requiring RAM availability >40GB. If you have any thoughts on what might be causing this problem or how to troubleshoot the issue, I'd very much appreciate your advice. Thanks!

I can't comment on Arlequin as I haven't personally used it in years and have never seen any source code for it. For R, I can tell you why errors are being thrown.

There are choose(n, 2) comparisons in a distance matrix (about (n*n)/2). The way poppr calculates the distance matrix is to first calculate the distance at each locus separately and then take the sum, which means that you end up needing a matrix that is m * choose(n, 2). When you set within = TRUE, n gets doubled (see documentation for poppr.amova).

Here's an illustration of how big these matrices can get:

library("memuse")
# Data set 1: within = FALSE
howbig(choose(14138, 2), 14, type = "double")
#> 10.424 GiB
# Data set 1: within = TRUE
howbig(choose(14138 * 2, 2), 14, type = "double")
#> 41.697 GiB
# Data set 2: within = FALSE
howbig(choose(46523, 2), 14, type = "double")
#> 112.879 GiB
# Data set 2: within = TRUE
howbig(choose(46523 * 2, 2), 14, type = "double")
#> 451.522 GiB

As you can see, they can get quite large. I haven't gotten around to improving this because it hasn't really been an issue before (not many people will have microsatellites genotyped for > 10k samples, but with simulations getting easier and easier, I should be expecting this).

I may have a couple of solutions that you can take or leave:

If you don't absolutely need to account for within-individual variance:

 - use the `dist()` function on the data
 - If that doesn't work, separate your data by locus, create an empty distance matrix, loop over the loci, calculate the distance, add that to the matrix, remove the temporary matrix, and run gc(). This reduces m to be 2.

If you do need to account for within-individual variance:

I say this with a bit of trepidation: there is an internal function called pool_haplotypes. This is what poppr.amova uses when within = TRUE to split diploid data into haplotypes. If you want to, you can use this internal function to split your data into haplotypes before doing the steps above, but be aware that this function may change without notice. Note, however, this may not solve your problems for your 46k data set:

howbig(choose(14138 * 2, 2), 2, type = "double")
#> 5.957 GiB
howbig(choose(46523 * 2, 2), 2, type = "double")
#> 64.503 GiB

That being said, all of this is only considering the poppr side of the equation (distance calculation), it does not necessarily consider what happens on the ade4 side.

I hope that answers your question. Feel free to follow up if I haven't!

--Zhian

messages.subject: poppr version 2.4.1 released
messages.body_plain:
Poppr version 2.4.1 has officially been released and is on CRAN. This update is strongly recommended.

For details, see https://github.com/grunwaldlab/poppr/releases/tag/v.2.4.1

To update on your system, simply enter into your R console:

install.packages("poppr", repos = "https://cran.rstudio.com")

Once you update, please ensure that your version is 2.4.1 and not 2.4.0

This version contains new features such as jack.ia(), which will randomly subset your data and calculate the index of association, color graphs for mlg.table(), and a completely overhauled psex() calculation with method = "multiple". In addition, genlight/snpclone objects will now have MLGs calculated via distance-based methods automatically (which is different from previous behavior where they were initially considered unique and you had to use mlg.filter() to delineate them).

Several important bugs were fixed in this version, which included several fixes to read.genalex(), fix_replen(),  win.ia(), and all functions that utilize round-robin allele frequencies rraf() with multiple populations.

Cheers,
Zhian

messages.body_plain:
I am using poppr for the first time and I am also new to R. I have non stratified data, 27 microsattellite loci and 260 individuals.

While performing DAPC analysis I got following:
details;

library("adegenet")
data(genalex)
pop(genalex) <- genalex$other$epid
dapc.genalex <- dapc(genalex, var.contrib = TRUE, scale = FALSE, n.pca = 30, n.da = nPop(genalex) - 1)
scatter(dapc.genalex, cell = 0, pch = 18:23, cstar = 0, mstree = TRUE, lwd = 2, lty = 2)

Error:
Error in dapc.genind(genalex, var.contrib = TRUE, scale = FALSE, n.pca = 30,  :
  x does not include pre-defined populations, and `pop' is not provided
> scatter(dapc.genalex, cell = 0, pch = 18:23, cstar = 0, mstree = TRUE, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
Error in scatter(dapc.genalex, cell = 0, pch = 18:23, cstar = 0, mstree = TRUE,  :
  object 'dapc.genalex' not found

please provide solution
>

messages.subject: Re: Problem with reading Genalex file
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

>From the example you have shown, it does not appear that you have imported your data. If you have your data in genalex format, you can use read.genalex("/path/to/file"), where you replace "/path/to/file" with the actual path to your data on your computer.

Additionally, it is important to note that dapc is a function from adegenet. I have seen a few citations for poppr floating around that use dapc and do not cite adegenet.

The data() function is for use with examples only. These examples live within the package, so using data(genalex) should have no effect. In fact, your script should render an error on line three.

Please read through the DAPC tutorial found here: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/wiki/Tutorials for information on the error. To conduct DAPC, you must have pre-defined groups. If you don't have pre-defined groups/populations, you can use k-means clustering with find.clusters, but be careful with the downstream analyses as you do not want to fall into the trap of comparing the differentiation of pre-defined groups (See Meirmans, 2015 for details: http://www.molecularecologist.com/2015/05/conversation-starter-common-mistakes-in-population-genetics/).

Hope that helps,
Zhian
